title: Combustion reactions
html:
Guiding question

What are the challenges of using chemical energy to address our energy needs?

This topic is about where our energy comes from when we burn things: writing combustion equations, comparing fuels by how much energy they give and how much CO2 they release, and looking at alternatives (biofuels and fuel cells). It builds on R1.1 (ΔH, calorimetry) and R1.2 (ΔHc data, bond enthalpies), and leads into R3.2 (redox and cells).

R1.3.1 Combustion reactions

Combustion is the rapid, exothermic reaction of a substance with oxygen. Reactive metals, non-metals and organic compounds all undergo combustion when heated in oxygen. Combustion is always a redox reaction: the fuel is oxidized and oxygen is reduced.

Type of substanceProductExample equation
Reactive metalMetal oxide (basic, ionic)2Mg(s) + O2(g) → 2MgO(s)
4Fe(s) + 3O2(g) → 2Fe2O3(s)
Non-metalNon-metal oxide (acidic, covalent)S(s) + O2(g) → SO2(g)
4P(s) + 5O2(g) → P4O10(s)
HydrogenWater2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(l)
Hydrocarbon (complete)CO2 + H2OCH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l)
Alcohol (complete)CO2 + H2OC2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l)

The more reactive a metal is with acids or water, the more vigorously it burns. Magnesium burns with a brilliant white flame; copper and lead only form an oxide layer when heated; gold does not react with oxygen at all.

Fill in the class summary: some metals burn vigorously in air, for example magnesium. The products are metal oxides. Some metals form an oxide layer on their surface when heated, for example lead and copper. Some metals, for example gold, do not react with oxygen. Potassium burns very vigorously (with a lilac flame): you can write 4K(s) + O2(g) → 2K2O(s). (In excess oxygen potassium actually forms the superoxide KO2, but K2O is accepted in IB answers.)

The class demonstration of burning iron wool on a balance (see-saw) shows that the product is heavier than the iron, because oxygen atoms from the air have been added. This is a common question: mass increases when a metal burns in air.

Iron wool is heated on one end of a balanced metre rule (a see-saw). What happens to the iron end as the iron burns?

  1. It rises, because the iron loses mass as smoke
  2. It goes down, because oxygen atoms from the air combine with the iron
  3. It stays level, because mass is conserved within the iron
  4. It rises, because the hot air lifts it

The product, iron oxide, contains the original iron plus oxygen from the air, so it is heavier. Mass is conserved overall, but the oxygen was not on the balance before.

Write balanced equations for the oxidation of zinc, copper and lead, then reveal

2Zn(s) + O2(g) → 2ZnO(s); 2Cu(s) + O2(g) → 2CuO(s) (copper(II) oxide); 2Pb(s) + O2(g) → 2PbO(s). Iron: 4Fe(s) + 3O2(g) → 2Fe2O3(s).

Balancing combustion equations for organic compounds

Key point
  1. Balance C first (number of CO2 = number of C atoms).
  2. Balance H next (number of H2O = half the number of H atoms).
  3. Balance O last, counting all O atoms in the products. For an alcohol, subtract the one O atom already in the fuel before working out the O2 needed.
  4. Halves are fine (e.g. 13/2 O2). For an enthalpy of combustion equation the fuel must have a coefficient of 1; otherwise any whole-number multiple scores the mark.
Worked example

Butane: C4H10 → 4CO2 + 5H2O. O atoms needed = 8 + 5 = 13, so 13/2 O2.

C4H10(g) + 6½O2(g) → 4CO2(g) + 5H2O(l)   (or ×2: 2C4H10 + 13O2 → 8CO2 + 10H2O)

Butan-1-ol: C4H9OH → 4CO2 + 5H2O. O atoms in products = 13; one O is already in the alcohol, so 12 O atoms = 6O2.

C4H9OH(l) + 6O2(g) → 4CO2(g) + 5H2O(l)

More answers from the class task: C3H6 + 4½O2 → 3CO2 + 3H2O; C10H22 + 15½O2 → 10CO2 + 11H2O; C8H16 + 12O2 → 8CO2 + 8H2O; C3H7OH + 4½O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O; C8H17OH + 12O2 → 8CO2 + 9H2O.

Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons and are unreactive towards acids, bases and most oxidizing agents, but they are very flammable, which is why they are good fuels. Within a homologous series, the larger the molecule, the more energy is released per mole on combustion (each extra CH2 adds roughly 650 kJ mol−1).

Which is the correctly balanced equation for the complete combustion of propan-1-ol?

  1. C3H7OH + 4O2 → 3CO2 + 3H2O
  2. C3H7OH + 4½O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O
  3. C3H7OH + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O
  4. C3H7OH + 4½O2 → 3CO2 + 3H2O

C3H7OH has 8 H atoms, so 4H2O. Product O atoms = 6 + 4 = 10; subtract the 1 O in the alcohol = 9 O atoms = 4½O2. Option C forgets the O in the alcohol.

What is the coefficient of O2 when one mole of decane, C10H22, burns completely?

  1. 10
  2. 11
  3. 15½
  4. 31

10CO2 + 11H2O contain 20 + 11 = 31 O atoms = 15½ O2.

title: Incomplete combustion
html:
R1.3.2 Incomplete combustion

When the oxygen supply is limited, organic compounds (especially hydrocarbons) undergo incomplete combustion, producing carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot) instead of carbon dioxide. Water is still formed. Longer-chain hydrocarbons are more likely to burn incompletely because they need much more oxygen per molecule.

CH4(g) + 1½O2(g) → CO(g) + 2H2O(l)    CH4(g) + O2(g) → C(s) + 2H2O(l)
C4H10 + 4½O2 → 4CO + 5H2O    C3H7OH + 3O2 → 3CO + 4H2O
Exam tipFor "write an equation for incomplete combustion", the safest answer has CO and H2O as products. Any correctly balanced combination of C, CO, CO2 and H2O is accepted, as long as it uses less oxygen than complete combustion.

Consequences of incomplete combustion:

  • Less energy is released per mole of fuel, because the carbon is not fully oxidized (C → CO releases much less energy than C → CO2).
  • Carbon monoxide is toxic: it is colourless and odourless and binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells far more strongly than oxygen, so blood carries less oxygen. The binding is very strong but not truly permanent; CO is only slowly released.
  • Carbon particulates (soot) give a smoky yellow flame (like a Bunsen burner with the air hole closed), blacken surfaces, worsen asthma and other respiratory problems, and can be carcinogenic.

In the lab, complete combustion products can be shown by drawing the gases through a cooled U-tube (water condenses; turns anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue or cobalt chloride paper pink) and then through limewater (turns cloudy with CO2).

Which is a correctly balanced equation for the incomplete combustion of propan-1-ol?

  1. C3H7OH + 2½O2 → 3CO + 3H2O
  2. C3H7OH + 3O2 → 3CO + 4H2O
  3. C3H7OH + 3½O2 → 3CO + 4H2O
  4. C3H7OH + 4½O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O

Products 3CO + 4H2O contain 3 + 4 = 7 O atoms; subtract the 1 in the alcohol = 6 O atoms = 3O2. Option D is complete combustion.

Write incomplete combustion equations (forming CO) for butane, propene, decane, butan-1-ol and octan-1-ol, then reveal

C4H10 + 4½O2 → 4CO + 5H2O
C3H6 + 3O2 → 3CO + 3H2O
C10H22 + 10½O2 → 10CO + 11H2O
C4H9OH + 4O2 → 4CO + 5H2O
C8H17OH + 8O2 → 8CO + 9H2O

Always balance C and H first, then O, remembering the O already in an alcohol.

Why is carbon monoxide toxic?

  1. It reacts with water in the lungs to form an acid
  2. It binds to haemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen, reducing oxygen transport
  3. It absorbs infrared radiation in the blood
  4. It oxidizes red blood cells

CO forms carboxyhaemoglobin, so less haemoglobin is free to carry O2. Because it is colourless and odourless, CO detectors are needed.

title: Fossil fuels and energy from fuels
html:
R1.3.3 Fossil fuels

Fossil fuels (coal, crude oil and natural gas) formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient organisms, under heat and pressure. They are non-renewable: they are used much faster than they form. Natural gas is mostly methane; crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons separated by fractional distillation into fractions of similar boiling point (refinery gas, petrol/gasoline, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen). Coal is mostly carbon, with aromatic hydrocarbons, water and minerals (including sulfur compounds).

FuelAdvantagesDisadvantages
CoalLarge reserves spread across the world; cheap; easy to store and transport as a solidMost CO2 released per unit of energy; produces SO2 (acid rain), soot and ash; mining is dangerous and damages land; lowest specific energy of the three
Crude oil (petrol, diesel, kerosene)Liquid fractions have a high energy density, ideal for transport; easy to move by pipeline; also a feedstock for plastics, medicinesLimited reserves concentrated in some regions (political/price issues); oil spills; CO2, CO, NOx and unburnt hydrocarbons from engines
Natural gas (CH4)Highest specific energy; burns cleanly (little soot or SO2); least CO2 per kJLow energy density unless compressed or liquefied; leaks of methane (a powerful greenhouse gas); explosion risk; finite
DefinitionA hydrocarbon is a compound of carbon and hydrogen only. Fractional distillation separates a mixture into its components on the basis of their different boiling points. A fraction is a mixture of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points and similar numbers of carbon atoms.

Why do some fuels release more energy? (H : C ratio)

The energy released depends on how much the fuel can still be oxidized. Carbon atoms with more hydrogen attached are in a lower oxidation state, so they release more energy when oxidized to CO2. The higher the H : C ratio, the more energy is released per gram and the less CO2 per kJ. The ratio falls from natural gas (CH4, H : C = 4) through petroleum (about 2, mostly –CH2– units) to coal (about 1 or less). Fuels that already contain oxygen, such as ethanol, are already partly oxidized and so release less energy per gram than hydrocarbons.

Specific energy and energy density

DefinitionSpecific energy is the energy released per unit mass of fuel (kJ g−1 or MJ kg−1). Energy density is the energy released per unit volume of fuel (kJ cm−3 or MJ dm−3).
specific energy = |ΔHc| ÷ M     energy density = specific energy × density = |ΔHc| × ρ ÷ M
Worked example

Liquefied propane (LPG): ΔHc = −2202 kJ mol−1, M = 44.10 g mol−1, density = 0.493 g cm−3.

Specific energy = 2202 ÷ 44.10 = 49.9 kJ g−1 (= 49.9 MJ kg−1).

Energy density = 49.9 kJ g−1 × 0.493 g cm−3 = 24.6 kJ cm−3 (= 24.6 MJ dm−3).

Check the units: kJ g−1 × g cm−3 = kJ cm−3. Energy density must be smaller than specific energy for any fuel less dense than 1 g cm−3.

Fossil fuels have high specific energy and (for liquids) high energy density, so a car can carry enough fuel for a long range in a small tank. A modern petrol or diesel car can travel around 800 miles on a tank. This, plus the existing refuelling infrastructure, is why they are still dominant for transport. Hydrogen has a very high specific energy but a very low energy density as a gas, so it must be compressed or liquefied, which costs energy. When comparing fuels, the energy needed to produce them (drilling, refining, harvesting, transport, cleaning up pollution) should also be subtracted from the energy they release.

Calculate the specific energy of octane, in kJ g−1. ΔHc = −5470 kJ mol−1, M = 114.26 g mol−1.

Specific energy = 5470 ÷ 114.26 = 47.9 kJ g−1 (= 47.9 MJ kg−1). Dividing kJ by kg instead of g would multiply by 1000, so the number in MJ kg−1 is the same.

Ethanol: ΔHc = −1367 kJ mol−1, density 0.785 g cm−3, M = 46.08 g mol−1. Calculate the energy density in kJ cm−3.

Specific energy = 1367 ÷ 46.08 = 29.67 kJ g−1. Energy density = 29.67 × 0.785 = 23.3 kJ cm−3 (23.3 MJ dm−3).

A biodiesel has M = 299 g mol−1, density 0.850 g cm−3 and enthalpy of combustion −12.0 MJ mol−1. Calculate its energy density in kJ cm−3.

Specific energy = 12 000 kJ mol−1 ÷ 299 g mol−1 = 40.1 kJ g−1. Energy density = 40.1 × 0.850 = 34.1 kJ cm−3. Convert MJ to kJ first.

Comparing the CO2 released by different fuels

The syllabus asks you to evaluate how much CO2 different fuels add to the atmosphere. Compare them on the same basis: per mole of CO2, per kJ, or per gram of fuel.

FuelΔHc / kJ mol−1Specific energy / kJ g−1Energy per mol CO2 / kJCO2 per MJ / g
Hydrogen, H2−286142— (no CO2)0
Methane, CH4−89155.589149
Octane, C8H18−547047.968464
Ethanol, C2H5OH−136729.768464
Coal (as carbon, C)−39432.8394112

Natural gas releases the most energy per mole of CO2, and coal the least, so switching from coal to gas reduces CO2 emissions for the same energy output.

Worked example

Calculate the mass of CO2 produced when 1.00 kg of octane burns completely.

n(C8H18) = 1000 ÷ 114.26 = 8.75 mol. Each mole gives 8 mol CO2: n(CO2) = 70.0 mol. Mass = 70.0 × 44.01 = 3.08 kg. The CO2 is heavier than the fuel because each carbon atom picks up two oxygen atoms from the air.

Which fuel releases the most energy per mole of CO2 produced?

  1. Coal (carbon)
  2. Octane
  3. Ethanol
  4. Methane

Methane: 891 kJ per mol CO2 (one C, four H). Coal gives only 394 kJ per mol CO2, because it has almost no hydrogen to oxidize.

title: The greenhouse effect and pollution
html:
R1.3.3 The greenhouse effect and climate change

Burning fossil fuels pollutes the environment. Carbon dioxide is always given off when fossil fuels burn; it is an essential, natural part of the atmosphere, but its rising concentration is causing climate change. Activities that do not release carbon dioxide overall are called carbon neutral.

  1. The Sun emits mostly short-wavelength radiation (visible and UV), which passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface.
  2. The warm surface re-emits energy as longer-wavelength infrared (IR) radiation.
  3. Greenhouse gases (H2O, CO2, CH4, N2O) absorb some of this IR. Their bonds vibrate (stretch or bend) in a way that changes the molecule's dipole moment, so they can absorb IR. N2 and O2 cannot.
  4. The gases re-emit the IR in all directions, including back towards the Earth, so the lower atmosphere is warmer than it would otherwise be.

The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life. The enhanced greenhouse effect is the extra warming caused by human activities raising greenhouse gas concentrations, mainly CO2 from burning fossil fuels and methane from agriculture and gas leaks. Most scientists agree it is causing global warming and climate change: rising sea levels, melting ice, more extreme weather, ocean acidification (CO2 dissolving to form carbonic acid) and changes to ecosystems. Warmer air also holds more water vapour, which is itself a greenhouse gas, so the effect amplifies itself (positive feedback).

Pollutant from burning fuelsHow it formsProblem caused
CO2Complete combustion of any carbon-based fuelMain greenhouse gas from human activity; ocean acidification
COIncomplete combustionToxic; reduces oxygen transport in blood
C (particulates)Very incomplete combustionRespiratory problems, asthma, possibly cancer; global dimming
Unburnt hydrocarbonsEvaporation of fuel or failure to burnGreenhouse gases; contribute to photochemical smog
NOx (NO, NO2)N2 and O2 from the air react at the high temperatures in enginesAcid rain (forms HNO3); photochemical smog
SO2Sulfur impurities in fuels (especially coal) burnAcid rain (forms H2SO3/H2SO4); respiratory irritant
Common mistakeDo not confuse the greenhouse effect with ozone depletion. The greenhouse effect involves IR radiation being absorbed by gases such as CO2; ozone depletion involves UV radiation and gases such as CFCs. Also, "the greenhouse effect" by itself is natural and necessary; it is the enhanced effect that is the problem.

Why can CO2 absorb infrared radiation while N2 cannot?

  1. CO2 is heavier than N2
  2. CO2 has vibrations that change its dipole moment; N2 has none
  3. CO2 has a permanent dipole
  4. N2 has a triple bond that is too strong to vibrate

CO2 is non-polar overall, but its asymmetric stretch and bending vibrations create a changing dipole, which is what allows IR absorption. The single stretch of N2 or O2 produces no dipole change.

Which pollutant from a car engine forms when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at high temperature?

  1. CO
  2. SO2
  3. NOx
  4. Particulates

N2 + O2 → 2NO happens only at the very high temperatures inside engines. NOx contributes to acid rain and photochemical smog.

Outline two pieces of evidence that link global warming to increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, then reveal

Any two: a strong correlation between atmospheric CO2 concentration and average global temperature over time; laboratory evidence that CO2 and other greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation; ice-core data (trapped air bubbles) showing CO2 and temperature rising and falling together; tree-ring, ocean-sediment and coral-reef records; computer models that only reproduce recent warming when human emissions are included.

title: Biofuels
html:
R1.3.4 Biofuels

Renewable energy sources are replaced naturally on a short timescale (biofuels, solar, wind); non-renewable sources will eventually run out (fossil fuels, nuclear fuels).

Biofuels are fuels made from recently living material (biomass). The carbon in them was fixed from atmospheric CO2 by photosynthesis over a short period of time (months or years, not millions of years).

Photosynthesis: 6CO2(g) + 6H2O(l) → C6H12O6(aq) + 6O2(g)   (endothermic; light energy absorbed by chlorophyll)

Bioethanol is made by fermentation of sugars or starch (from sugar cane, corn, wheat) by yeast, in aqueous solution, at about 35–37 °C, under anaerobic conditions:

C6H12O6(aq) → 2C2H5OH(aq) + 2CO2(g)

Other biofuels include biodiesel (made by reacting vegetable oils or animal fats, which are triglyceride esters, with methanol in the presence of a base catalyst: transesterification), biogas (mainly methane, from anaerobic decay of waste) and wood.

Worked example

Why is bioethanol described as (nearly) carbon neutral? Follow one mole of glucose:

  • Photosynthesis removes 6 mol CO2 from the air to make 1 mol glucose.
  • Fermentation releases 2 mol CO2 and gives 2 mol ethanol.
  • Burning 2 mol ethanol (C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O) releases 4 mol CO2.

Total released = 2 + 4 = 6 mol = total absorbed. In practice it is not fully carbon neutral, because fossil fuels are used for farm machinery, fertilizer production, distillation of the ethanol and transport.

Advantages of biofuelsDisadvantages of biofuels
Renewable: crops can be regrownLand used for fuel crops cannot grow food: may raise food prices ("food vs fuel")
Lower net CO2 emissions (close to carbon neutral)Deforestation to create farmland releases CO2 and reduces biodiversity
Can use waste materials (biogas, used cooking oil)Lower specific energy than petrol (ethanol 29.7 vs octane 47.9 kJ g−1), so more fuel is needed
Reduces dependence on imported oil; can be produced locallyFertilizers, water use and processing need energy; engines may need modifying for high ethanol blends
Ethanol burns more cleanly (less soot) and can be blended with petrol (gasohol)Ethanol absorbs water (it is hygroscopic) and can corrode some engine parts
Exam tip"Discuss" questions on biofuels want a balanced answer: give at least one advantage and one disadvantage, and link the CO2 argument to photosynthesis. The ethical points (land use, poor farmers growing fuel crops instead of food) also score.

Which conditions are used to make ethanol by fermentation?

  1. Concentrated H2SO4, 300 °C, high pressure
  2. Yeast, aqueous solution, about 37 °C, no oxygen
  3. Yeast, 100 °C, plenty of oxygen
  4. Platinum catalyst, gaseous glucose

Yeast enzymes work best at about 35–37 °C (higher temperatures denature them), in solution, and anaerobically; with oxygen, the yeast respire the sugar to CO2 instead. (Making ethanol from ethene uses steam with an acid catalyst, H3PO4, at high temperature and pressure.)

How many moles of CO2 are absorbed by photosynthesis to make the glucose that, after fermentation, gives 2 mol of ethanol?

6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2, and one glucose gives two ethanol. So 6 mol CO2 absorbed, matching the 2 (fermentation) + 4 (combustion) released.

Discuss the environmental and ethical issues linked to decisions about using biofuels, then compare with this model answer

For: renewable; close to carbon neutral because the CO2 released was recently absorbed by photosynthesis; can use waste; reduces dependence on imported oil; local jobs. Against: land used for fuel crops is not used for food, raising food prices; poor farmers may be paid to grow fuel rather than food; deforestation and biodiversity loss; fertilizers, pesticides, water and fossil-fuel energy for farming, distillation and transport mean it is not truly carbon neutral; lower specific energy than petrol; engines may need adapting. A balanced conclusion weighs these, e.g. biofuels from waste avoid most of the drawbacks.

title: Fuel cells
html:
R1.3.5 Fuel cells

A fuel cell converts the chemical energy of a fuel and an oxidant (usually oxygen from air) directly into electrical energy. It works like a voltaic cell, but the reactants are supplied continuously from outside, so it does not run flat or need recharging, as long as fuel is supplied.

Fuel cells are electrochemical cells, like voltaic cells and electrolytic cells. The most common is the hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell. Both electrodes are made of porous carbon (full of tiny holes) containing a catalyst.

  • Oxidation happens at the anode (negative electrode in a voltaic or fuel cell); reduction happens at the cathode (positive). Mnemonic: AN OX, RED CAT.
  • Electrons flow through the external circuit from anode to cathode; ions move through the electrolyte to complete the circuit.
  • Electrodes are made of porous carbon (or metal) containing a catalyst, usually platinum, to give a large surface area and speed up the electrode reactions.
Fuel cellAnode (oxidation, −)Cathode (reduction, +)
Hydrogen, acidic electrolyte (proton exchange membrane)H2(g) → 2H+(aq) + 2e−O2(g) + 4H+(aq) + 4e− → 2H2O(l)
Hydrogen, alkaline electrolyte (KOH)H2(g) + 2OH−(aq) → 2H2O(l) + 2e−O2(g) + 2H2O(l) + 4e− → 4OH−(aq)
Methanol, acidic electrolyteCH3OH(aq) + H2O(l) → CO2(g) + 6H+(aq) + 6e−O2(g) + 4H+(aq) + 4e− → 2H2O(l)
Overall (hydrogen, either electrolyte): 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(l)    Overall (methanol): 2CH3OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 4H2O
Worked example

Deduce the half-equations for a methanol fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte.

  1. Methanol is oxidized to CO2: CH3OH → CO2.
  2. Balance O with H2O: CH3OH + H2O → CO2.
  3. Balance H with H+: CH3OH + H2O → CO2 + 6H+.
  4. Balance charge with electrons: CH3OH + H2O → CO2 + 6H+ + 6e− (anode).
  5. Cathode: O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O. Multiply the anode by 2 and the cathode by 3 so both involve 12e−, add and cancel to get the overall equation.

Step by step (acidic hydrogen cell):

  1. Hydrogen gas enters the anode chamber and is oxidized to H+, losing electrons to the anode: H2 → 2H+ + 2e−.
  2. The electrons pass along the external wire to the cathode (this is the electric current).
  3. H+ ions move through the electrolyte (membrane) to the cathode.
  4. At the cathode, H+ ions and electrons react with oxygen entering the cathode chamber: O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O.
  5. Water leaves through the outlet. Overall: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

How it works, in exam language: fuel enters the anode compartment and is oxidized, releasing electrons onto the anode; oxygen is reduced at the cathode, taking electrons. This sets up a potential difference between the electrodes, which drives electrons through the external circuit and generates electricity.

Advantages of hydrogen fuel cellsDisadvantages
Only product is water: no CO2, CO, NOx or particulates at the point of useMost hydrogen is currently made from fossil fuels (steam reforming of methane), which releases CO2; electrolysis needs a lot of electricity
More efficient than burning fuel in an engine (less energy wasted as heat)Hydrogen is hard to store and transport (low energy density; needs high pressure or very low temperature); flammable/explosive
Quiet, few moving parts; work continuously while fuel is suppliedExpensive platinum catalysts; few refuelling stations
Key pointFuel cell vs battery: a primary cell is used once; a secondary (rechargeable) cell stores energy and is recharged by reversing the reaction; a fuel cell stores no reactants itself and generates electricity only while fuel and oxygen flow in.

In a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, what happens at the anode?

  1. O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O
  2. H2 → 2H+ + 2e−
  3. H2 + 2OH− → 2H2O + 2e−
  4. 2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e−

Oxidation (loss of electrons) happens at the anode, and the fuel is what gets oxidized. Option C is the anode reaction in an alkaline cell.

Which statement about a hydrogen fuel cell is correct?

  1. Electrons flow through the electrolyte from anode to cathode
  2. It must be recharged when the reactants are used up
  3. It converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy while fuel is supplied
  4. The anode is the positive electrode

Electrons flow through the external wire, ions through the electrolyte. Fuel cells are refuelled, not recharged, and the anode is negative.

Predict first: write the two half-equations for a methanol fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte and combine them, then reveal

Anode: CH3OH + H2O → CO2 + 6H+ + 6e−. Cathode: O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O. ×2 and ×3 (12e− each), add and cancel: 2CH3OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 4H2O.

Common mistakes and exam tips

  • Forgetting the oxygen atom already in an alcohol when balancing its combustion equation.
  • Writing incomplete combustion products as CO2 + CO + H2O without checking the O balance. Keep it simple: CO + H2O.
  • Mixing up specific energy (per mass) and energy density (per volume). Check units.
  • Saying CO2 "destroys the ozone layer" or that greenhouse gases "trap UV". They absorb and re-emit IR.
  • Claiming biofuels are completely carbon neutral without mentioning the energy used to grow, process and transport them.
  • Putting oxidation at the cathode. In every cell, oxidation is at the anode.
